reason: The sources provide sufficient details and multiple-source verification for a surprising 45-second story about the Hindenburg disaster.
story: On May 6, 1937, the massive German airship Hindenburg attempted an evening landing at Lakehurst, New Jersey, after a delayed transatlantic flight. Filled with seven million cubic feet of flammable hydrogen, the airship suddenly caught fire near its stern. In roughly 32 seconds, the giant craft was incinerated and crashed to the ground. Yet, astonishingly, most of the 97 people on board survived the disaster. Fourteen-year-old cabin boy Werner Franz escaped unscathed after a burst ballast tank doused him in water, allowing him to jump to safety. Though 35 people tragically lost their lives—mostly due to the rapid inferno and structural collapse—over sixty individuals walked, jumped, or were rescued alive from the burning wreckage, bringing the golden era of commercial airships to an abrupt end.
angle: The Hindenburg disaster is remembered as a terrifying inferno that consumed the giant airship in about half a minute, yet most of the people on board actually survived.

claims.claim: The Hindenburg disaster occurred on May 6, 1937.

evidence.quote: The Hindenburg disaster was an airship accident that occurred on May 6, 1937, in Manchester Township, New Jersey, United States.
The Hindenburg disaster occurred on 6 May 1937 when the German Zeppelin airship LZ 129 Hindenburg attempted to land at Lakehurst, New Jersey, but burst into flames.

claims.claim: There were 35 fatalities among the people on board the airship.

evidence.quote: The accident caused 35 fatalities (13 passengers and 22 crewmen) among the 97 people on board (36 passengers and 61 crewmen), and an additional fatality on the ground.
35 people on board and one member of the ground crew died in the disaster; there were 62 survivors.

claims.claim: The airship disaster took approximately 32 seconds.

evidence.quote: The time that it took, from the first signs of disaster to the bow crashing to the ground, is reported as 32, 34, or 37 seconds.
The airship's gas cells were filled with highly flammable hydrogen gas, and the Hindenburg crashed to the ground in just 32 seconds.

claims.claim: Werner Franz was a 14-year-old cabin boy on the Hindenburg who survived the disaster.

evidence.quote: Werner Franz, the 14-year-old cabin boy, was initially dazed on realizing the ship was on fire but when a water tank above him burst open, putting out the fire around him, he was spurred to action.
So did 39 of its 61 crew members, including Werner Franz, a 14-year-old cabin boy.

claims.claim: The airship's gas cells were filled with hydrogen.

evidence.quote: Filled with hydrogen, it caught fire and was destroyed during its attempt to dock with its mooring mast at Naval Air Station Lakehurst.
The airship's gas cells were filled with highly flammable hydrogen gas, and the Hindenburg crashed to the ground in just 32 seconds.

claims.claim: Herbert Morrison recorded a famous radio eyewitness report for station WLS in Chicago.

evidence.quote: The disaster was the subject of newsreel coverage, photographs and Herbert Morrison's recorded radio eyewitness reports from the landing field, which were broadcast the next day.

Chicago radio station WLS had sent reporter Herb Morrison and sound engineer Charles Nehlsen to record the landing which was being celebrated as the first anniversary of the inauguration of transatlantic passenger service and the opening of the 1937 season.

claims.claim: An additional fatality occurred on the ground, identified as Allen Hagaman.

evidence.quote: The accident caused 35 fatalities (13 passengers and 22 crewmen) among the 97 people on board (36 passengers and 61 crewmen), and an additional fatality on the ground.

On May 6, 1937, while preparing to land at the Lakehurst Naval Air Station in New Jersey, the Hindenburg burst into flames and crashed to the ground, killing thirty-five of the ninety-seven people on board and one member of the ground crew.

claims.claim: Captain Max Pruss survived the crash with severe burns.

evidence.quote: First Officer Captain Albert Sammt found Captain Max Pruss trying to re-enter the wreckage to look for survivors. Pruss's face was badly burned, and he required months of hospitalization and reconstructive surgery, but he survived.
Captain Pruss was seriously injured but survived.

disputed: The exact cause of the initial spark is disputed, with theories including static electricity, sabotage, lightning, and engine backfires. A script should present static discharge as the leading scientific theory while acknowledging that sabotage was heavily suspected at the time.
